title: How doth the city sit (Lamentations 1:1)
hookLine: the city once full of people sits solitary, like a widow

lines: A CITY, DRAWN AS A WOMAN.
cards: A city, drawn as a woman, sitting on the ground. The streets around her used to be loud with people. Now nobody comes.
That's the opening picture of the book of Lamentations, and it begins with one sighing word, eichah, how. Earlier on this path we heard that word chanted on Tisha B'Av, the fast for the Temples.
Today we stay with the picture that follows it.

teach.b: The first verse, in the JPS 1917 translation: "How doth the city sit solitary, That was full of people! How is she become as a widow! She that was great among the nations, And princess among the provinces, How is she become tributary!"
Three pictures, one after another. Full of people, now alone. A wife, now a widow.

teach.h: A WIDOW, A PRINCESS PAYING TRIBUTE.
teach.b: A princess, now paying tribute. Each is a fall from a height, and each is about a person, not a pile of stones. Lamentations doesn't describe Jerusalem's ruins like a report.
It turns the city into someone you could sit beside.
Then it shows her at night: "She weepeth sore in the night, And her tears are on her cheeks; She hath none to comfort her Among all her lovers." Tears on her cheeks.
Not falling, just there, the way tears stay when no one has come to wipe them. The chapter keeps coming back to those words: none to comfort her. The book doesn't argue.
It doesn't hurry to explain why it happened, or how it will be fixed.
It sits. Eichah isn't a question waiting for an answer. It's a cry.
And the city's posture becomes the posture of the people who read it: on Tisha B'Av, mourners sit low, on the floor or on low stools, while the book is chanted.
Sometimes the honest thing a text can do is refuse to stand up too fast. And now someone is sitting with her: the one reading.

how: On Tisha B'Av, the fast for the destruction of the Temples, Lamentations is chanted in synagogue in a mournful melody while people sit on the floor or on low stools.

o: woe: a curse spoken over a city's enemies
how: the sighing first word of Lamentations
why: a question demanding God explain

games.q: how she sits alone — tap the pairs.

s: Lamentations opens by explaining why Jerusalem fell
it opens with a cry and a picture: a city sitting alone like a widow.
the first chapter keeps saying she has none to comfort her
the words come back again and again: no one to comfort her.
on Tisha B'Av, people sit low while Lamentations is chanted
on the floor or on low stools, keeping the city company.

games.q: you've come to a city in ruins. she's weeping in the night, tears on her cheeks. what do you do first?
o: promise it will all be rebuilt soon.
games.why: Lamentations doesn't hurry to explain or fix. it sits, and so do those who chant it on Tisha B'Av.

practice: Find a quiet room if you can, or turn away from the screens around you, and sit down.
Notice the quiet and what's missing from it, voices, footsteps, someone who used to be there, and don't fill it; if a loss comes to mind, yours or the world's, let it sit beside you.
If you pray, let the silence be part of your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Eichah. The sighing word that opens Lamentations: Jerusalem, once full of people, sitting alone like a widow. Today's word.
